learn.title: Solar Windows in Buildings 🌞
learn.intro: Building Integrated Photovoltaics (BIPV) turns roofs, walls, and windows into solar panels, blending clean energy generation with architecture. This innovation reduces reliance on traditional solar farms, saving land and enhancing building aesthetics while cutting carbon emissions. BIPV is key to achieving net-zero cities by making solar energy seamless and visually unobtrusive.
learn.c1_text: BIPV integrates solar cells directly into building materials like glass or roofing tiles. For example, a single BIPV panel on a 100m² roof can generate ~3-5 kW of power daily, equivalent to powering 2-3 homes. Unlike rooftop panels, BIPV doesn’t require extra space, making it ideal for urban areas where land is scarce.
learn.c2_text: Cities like Mumbai and Bangalore are adopting BIPV for commercial buildings. The National Institute of Solar Energy (NISE) reports that BIPV can reduce a building’s electricity bills by 40-60%. By 2030, India aims to install 40 GW of rooftop solar, with BIPV contributing significantly to this target through innovative designs.
learn.c3_text: India’s BIPV market is projected to reach $2 billion by 2025. The government’s Solar Rooftop Mission offers subsidies for BIPV installations, encouraging adoption in schools and offices. For instance, the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) campuses use BIPV to cut grid dependence by 70% annually.
learn.stat1: India installed 30 GW of rooftop solar in 2024, with BIPV contributing 5% of this total.
learn.stat2: BIPV systems can last 25+ years with minimal maintenance.
learn.stat3: A 1 kW BIPV system costs ~₹1.5 lakhs in India.
learn.stat4: BIPV reduces urban heat island effects by 15% in pilot projects.

learn.title: Wind Turbine Blades 🌀
learn.intro: Wind turbines convert kinetic energy from wind into electricity using rotating blades and generators. This technology is vital for scaling renewable energy, as wind is abundant and free. Modern turbines can power entire cities, making wind energy a cornerstone of the global transition to clean power.
learn.c1_text: Turbine blades are designed to capture wind efficiently. A 2 MW turbine’s blades can spin at 10-20 rotations per minute, generating ~6,000 kWh monthly. The blade shape (aerodynamic airfoil) ensures maximum energy extraction even at low wind speeds, like 12 km/h.
learn.c2_text: The rotor spins a generator, converting mechanical energy to electricity. A typical 5 MW turbine uses a permanent magnet generator, producing 4.5-5 MW annually at 30% capacity factor. This is enough to power 4,000 Indian homes yearly, showcasing wind’s scalability.
learn.c3_text: India’s rural areas use small wind turbines (up to 100 kW) for irrigation and lighting. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) reports 500+ small wind projects in states like Tamil Nadu, reducing diesel use by 30% in villages. These systems cost ~₹3-5 lakhs and have a 15-year lifespan.
learn.stat1: India has 1.5 GW of small wind capacity, serving 500,000+ rural households.
learn.stat2: A 50 kW turbine can save ₹1.2 lakhs annually in electricity costs.
learn.stat3: Small wind turbines require minimal land, ideal for farms.
learn.stat4: Wind speeds in Rajasthan average 6 m/s, optimal for small turbines.

learn.title: Power Purchase Agreements 💰
learn.intro: A Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) is a contract where a developer sells renewable energy to a buyer at a fixed price. This financing model reduces upfront costs for projects, accelerating renewable adoption. PPAs are crucial for India’s solar and wind growth, enabling corporations and utilities to lock in clean energy without upfront investment.
learn.c1_text: In a PPA, a developer builds a solar farm and agrees to sell electricity to a buyer (e.g., a factory) for 20 years. For example, a 10 MW solar PPA in Gujarat might cost ₹4.50/kWh, lower than grid prices. The developer handles maintenance, while the buyer pays a stable rate, ensuring predictable energy costs.
learn.c2_text: Developers avoid bank loans, reducing financial risk. Buyers get cheaper, sustainable power. In 2023, Indian corporations signed 2 GW of PPAs, saving ₹5,000 crores annually. This model also attracts foreign investment, as seen in Rajasthan’s solar parks.
learn.c3_text: India’s PPA market grew 40% in 2023, with 15 GW+ under contract. The government’s Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme boosts PPAs by offering subsidies. For instance, Tata Power’s 500 MW solar PPA in Madhya Pradesh powers 100,000 homes at 18% lower costs than grid electricity.
learn.stat1: India’s PPA market reached $15 billion in 2024.
learn.stat2: PPAs reduce project risk by 60% compared to traditional financing.
learn.stat3: A 1 MW solar PPA in India costs ~₹3.5 lakhs/kWh.
learn.stat4: Corporate PPAs in India grew 50% year-on-year in 2024.

learn.title: Hydrogen Colors 🌈
learn.intro: Hydrogen is categorized by color based on production methods: grey (fossil fuels), blue (captured carbon), and green (renewables). This color code helps distinguish sustainability. Green hydrogen, produced via renewable-powered electrolysis, is critical for decarbonizing industries like steel and transport, aligning with India’s net-zero goals.
learn.c1_text: Grey hydrogen uses coal or gas without carbon capture, emitting CO2. Green hydrogen uses solar/wind to split water, emitting zero CO2. For example, producing 1 ton of grey hydrogen emits 9-12 tons of CO2, while green hydrogen emits none. India’s target is 5 million tons of green hydrogen by 2030.
learn.c2_text: Blue hydrogen adds carbon capture to grey production, reducing emissions by 90%. It’s a bridge technology until green scales. In India, blue hydrogen projects in Gujarat aim to produce 100,000 tons/year by 2025, supported by IEA funding.
learn.c3_text: India’s Hydrogen Mission targets 5 GW of green hydrogen production by 2030. States like Tamil Nadu and Gujarat are piloting projects. For instance, a green hydrogen plant in Tamil Nadu uses 100 MW of solar to produce 30,000 tons/year, cutting industrial emissions by 15%.
learn.stat1: India imports 90% of its hydrogen, costing ₹150/kg.
learn.stat2: Green hydrogen production costs ₹200-300/kg in India (target: ₹100/kg by 2030).
learn.stat3: Blue hydrogen reduces emissions by 90% vs grey.
learn.stat4: India’s Hydrogen Mission allocated ₹19,744 crores in 2024.

learn.title: Reusing EV Batteries ♻️
learn.intro: Second-life EV batteries repurpose used car batteries for grid storage. This extends battery life by 10-15 years, reducing waste and costs. In India, this approach is gaining traction as EV adoption rises, offering a sustainable solution for managing battery disposal and supporting renewable energy integration.
learn.c1_text: EV batteries lose 20-30% capacity after 8-10 years but still retain 70-80% efficiency for grid use. For example, a 60 kWh EV battery can store 40 kWh for the grid. This reduces the need for new batteries, cutting costs by 40% and waste by millions of tons annually.
learn.c2_text: Second-life batteries stabilize grids by storing excess solar/wind energy. In India, a 1 MW second-life battery project in Maharashtra can provide 4 hours of backup power for 500 homes. This helps integrate 50% more renewables into the grid without new infrastructure.
learn.c3_text: Startups like Urban Circuit in India are deploying second-life batteries in cities. The Ministry of Power supports this with subsidies. For instance, a 500 kWh second-life battery system in Delhi cuts grid reliance by 30% for a commercial building, saving ₹2 lakhs/year.
learn.stat1: India plans to repurpose 100,000 EV batteries by 2025.
learn.stat2: Second-life batteries cost 30-50% less than new ones.
learn.stat3: A 100 kWh second-life battery lasts 10 years in grid use.
learn.stat4: India’s EV battery recycling market is expected to reach $1.2 billion by 2030.

learn.title: Mini Wind Turbines for Homes 🏠
learn.intro: Small wind turbines generate electricity for homes or communities using compact designs. They’re ideal for rural areas with consistent wind. In India, these turbines power farms, schools, and villages, reducing diesel use and providing affordable, clean energy. They’re a step toward decentralized renewable energy systems.
learn.c1_text: Mini turbines (up to 100 kW) spin small blades to generate power. A 10 kW turbine can produce 300-500 kWh/month, enough for a small home. They operate at wind speeds of 12-20 km/h, making them suitable for Indian plains like Punjab or Gujarat.
learn.c2_text: In Rajasthan, a 20 kW turbine powers a dairy farm, saving ₹1.5 lakhs/year in diesel costs. Schools in Odisha use 5 kW turbines for lighting and computers. These systems are modular, allowing communities to scale capacity as needed.
learn.c3_text: India has 1.5 GW of small wind capacity, serving 500,000+ households. The MNRE offers subsidies covering 40% of costs. For example, a 50 kW turbine in Tamil Nadu costs ~₹2.5 lakhs after subsidy, with a 15-year payback period.
learn.stat1: Small wind turbines in India cost ₹3-5 lakhs after subsidies.
learn.stat2: They reduce diesel use by 30-50% in rural areas.
learn.stat3: A 50 kW turbine can power 10-15 homes daily.
learn.stat4: Wind speeds in Rajasthan average 6 m/s, ideal for small turbines.
